reference.source: Kelley & Firestein's Textbook of Rheumatology / vascular surgery guidance
clinicalPearls: A subset of abdominal aortic aneurysms with a markedly thickened, inflamed wall and surrounding fibrosis
Classically presents with the triad of chronic abdominal or back pain, weight loss, and a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate
CT shows a thickened aneurysm wall with a periaortic soft-tissue cuff that typically spares the posterior wall
Adjacent structures such as the ureters and duodenum may be encased, causing obstruction
It overlaps with chronic periaortitis and IgG4-related disease in some patients
Inflammatory markers are frequently elevated, unlike in ordinary atherosclerotic aneurysm
Surgical or endovascular repair follows standard aneurysm size and symptom thresholds, with attention to the inflammatory tissue
reference.pathophysiology: Inflammatory abdominal aortic aneurysm is characterised by a dense chronic inflammatory and fibrotic reaction in the aneurysm wall and surrounding retroperitoneum, superimposed on aneurysmal degeneration. Transmural lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, medial destruction, and adventitial fibrosis thicken the wall and generate a periaortic inflammatory mass that can entrap the ureters and bowel. The process shares features with chronic periaortitis and, in some cases, IgG4-related disease, and the inflammation contributes to pain, systemic symptoms, and adhesion of adjacent structures.
additionalInvestigations: CT or MR angiography demonstrating wall thickening and a periaortic cuff
Inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein)
Serum IgG4 to assess for an IgG4-related component
Renal function and urinary tract imaging for ureteric obstruction
PET imaging in selected cases to gauge inflammatory activity
Blood cultures when infective aneurysm must be excluded
redFlags: Sudden severe pain or haemodynamic instability suggesting rupture
Obstructive uropathy with deteriorating renal function
Features suggesting infective aetiology such as fever and positive cultures
reference.prognosis: Repair of the aneurysm carries the usual operative considerations, and the periaortic inflammation often regresses afterwards; where an underlying inflammatory or IgG4-related process persists, immunosuppression and surveillance are added. Overall prognosis after treatment is generally good, though ureteric involvement may need separate management.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a simple degenerative aneurysm and missing the periaortic inflammation
Overlooking ureteric entrapment and obstructive uropathy
Failing to consider IgG4-related disease as an underlying cause
Not excluding an infective (mycotic) aneurysm before assuming inflammation is sterile
references: Society for Vascular Surgery aortic aneurysm guidance
management: Repair the aneurysm by open surgery or endovascular aneurysm repair according to size, morphology and rupture risk
Suppress the periaortic inflammation with corticosteroids, adding steroid-sparing immunosuppression or rituximab where an IgG4-related or chronic periaortitis component persists
Relieve ureteric obstruction with ureteric stenting or ureterolysis to protect renal function
Control cardiovascular risk factors with antihypertensives, statin therapy and smoking cessation
Monitor with serial cross-sectional imaging, inflammatory markers and renal function to track regression of the inflammatory cuff and detect complications
Manage jointly with vascular surgery and rheumatology, escalating to urgent repair for symptoms suggesting expansion or rupture
